subject: Economics
title: Paper II - Economics of Pakistan (100 Marks)

segments.text: This paper is not a list of statistics to memorize. Use the economic theory built up in Paper I to explain Pakistan’s structural issues, institutions, and policy choices, and only then support that analysis with current official evidence — the Pakistan Economic Survey, the Federal Budget, State Bank publications, and current IMF/World Bank material. A single reliable habit runs through every topic here: separate the long-run structural story (which changes slowly) from the latest yearly movement (which changes constantly), so a temporary number never gets mistaken for the underlying explanation.

blocks.text: A. Measuring Development, Growth versus Redistribution, and Poverty

segments.text: Measuring development asks whether people are becoming more productive, secure, and capable, not merely whether nominal output is rising. Common indicators span real GDP per capita, productivity, poverty rates, employment, health, education, inequality, and composite human-development measures. “Underdevelopment” is best analyzed through specific structural constraints rather than used as a vague label: low tax-collection capacity, weak learning outcomes, unreliable energy supply, low productivity, and limited formal-sector employment tend to reinforce one another, which is why development problems in practice often arrive as a connected cluster rather than a single isolated weakness.

Growth expands the overall size of the economy; redistributive justice concerns how the resulting opportunities, burdens, and gains are actually shared. Badly designed policy can create real trade-offs between the two, but growth and inclusion can also reinforce each other, when education, health, fair competition, and social protection raise overall productivity rather than merely redistributing a fixed pie. Example: a subsidy can genuinely help a vulnerable group, but if poorly targeted it can also become fiscally very costly; well-targeted support can protect the same group at a meaningfully lower budget cost — so the productive framing of this debate is efficiency plus equity plus fiscal sustainability together, not “growth or justice” treated as strict opposites.

Absolute poverty compares a person’s resources against a fixed minimum standard; relative poverty compares them against the living standard of the wider society at the same time. The basic-needs approach emphasizes guaranteed minimum access to essentials such as food, shelter, health, and education. Sustainable development means meeting present needs without undermining future generations’ capacity to meet their own — and environmental degradation is very much an economic-development problem, not a separate topic: polluted water, for instance, can raise disease incidence and treatment costs while directly reducing worker productivity.

blocks.text: B. Planning Experience, Agriculture, and Industry

segments.text: Economic planning in Pakistan has moved through different plans, policy regimes, and institutional arrangements over time. The useful exam skill is not memorizing plan names in sequence, but judging each period’s goals, implementation, and actual outcomes together. Planning tends to fail when targets exceed administrative capacity, when policies are inconsistent over time, when incentives for implementers are weak, when projects are poorly selected, or when political or institutional instability disrupts continuity — a plan can contain entirely sound targets on paper yet still underperform if financing is uncertain or agencies fail to coordinate. Strong institutions improve implementation, monitoring, and accountability, which is why institutional quality is as important to development outcomes as the specific policy content of any given plan.

Agriculture matters for food security, rural incomes, employment, industrial inputs, and exports, and its performance depends jointly on water availability, seed quality, technology, land tenure arrangements, access to finance, functioning markets, and climate conditions. The Green Revolution raised yields substantially through improved seeds, expanded irrigation, and fertilizer use, but its benefits were distributed unevenly wherever farmers’ access to these inputs differed — a farmer with improved seed but unreliable irrigation and no affordable credit may still be unable to adopt the full technology package, illustrating why any single input improvement rarely transforms outcomes on its own. Land-reform debates in Pakistan’s history center on the tension between efficiency, equity, and tenure security, and cooperative farming has been proposed at various points as one way to combine small landholdings into more efficient production units.

Industrial policy asks how Pakistan built, and can further deepen, its manufacturing capacity, productivity, exports, and technological capability. Early import-substitution strategy protected domestic production behind tariff and other barriers, which can genuinely help a new industry learn and grow — but permanent protection also reduces the competitive pressure that would otherwise push firms toward efficiency, which is the central trade-off in any import-substitution debate. Nationalization expanded state ownership of industry substantially in the 1970s; subsequent privatization and deregulation moved policy in the opposite direction. Export-oriented firms, by contrast, face direct world competition and therefore need reliable energy, logistics, and product standards to compete internationally — a different and generally more demanding requirement than serving a protected domestic market alone.

blocks.text: C. External Sector, Privatization, and Islamic Banking

segments.text: Pakistan’s external sector depends jointly on exports, imports, services trade, remittances, capital flows, borrowing, and foreign-exchange reserves, and a persistent external gap can create sustained pressure on the exchange rate and on financing needs. The terms of trade compare export prices against import prices: if import prices rise sharply while export prices do not, the terms of trade deteriorate, meaning more exports are needed to pay for the same volume of imports as before. Remittances (money sent home by workers abroad) support household income and foreign-exchange availability, but they are not a substitute for genuine export competitiveness, since they depend on migration patterns and destination-country conditions rather than domestic productive capacity. Foreign aid and foreign investment can help finance development, but their real value depends on their cost, attached conditions, technology transfer, effect on productivity, and any repayment obligations involved — none of these forms of external financing should be treated as costless.

Privatization transfers ownership or control of a state enterprise or state assets to private investors; denationalization specifically reverses an earlier act of nationalization; deregulation reduces or redesigns state controls to increase competition or flexibility in a sector. The economic case for privatization typically includes efficiency gains, new investment, and fiscal relief for government, but the risks include weak competition, undervaluation of the asset sold, disruption to existing jobs, and — importantly — simply creating a private monopoly in place of a public one if the post-privatization regulatory framework is poor. Example: selling a monopoly without an effective regulator can replace a public monopoly with an equally uncompetitive private one, delivering none of the competitive benefits privatization is meant to produce. A sound process for evaluating any privatization requires transparency, genuine competition in the sale process, and a clear regulatory framework established afterward.

Islamic (interest-free) banking structures finance in accordance with Shariah principles, avoiding conventional interest-based lending in favour of approved sale, lease, partnership, and investment structures. Core contract types include mudarabah (a profit-sharing partnership), musharakah (a joint-venture partnership), murabaha (a cost-plus sale), ijara (a lease), and sukuk (an Islamic financial certificate functioning similarly to a bond but structured around an underlying asset). Example: in a murabaha structure, the bank purchases an asset and then sells it on to the customer at a disclosed mark-up under an agreed contract, rather than extending a conventional interest-bearing cash loan — the economic substance of financing an asset purchase is similar, but the legal and risk structure is genuinely different. A proper economic analysis of Islamic banking examines risk-sharing arrangements, the link to a real underlying asset, governance, liquidity management, and the regulatory transition involved, not merely the Arabic terminology for each contract type.

blocks.text: D. Energy, Social Sector Development, and a Connected Framework of Major Issues

segments.text: Energy policy aims to provide reliable, affordable, and sustainable energy while keeping the sector’s own finances viable. The major economic questions here include the generation fuel mix, fuel-import dependence, transmission and distribution losses, pricing policy, subsidies, circular debt (unpaid obligations accumulating through the energy supply chain when tariffs are held below actual cost without a properly funded subsidy), investment needs, sector governance, and the ongoing shift toward cleaner energy sources. Example: keeping tariffs below cost without a properly funded subsidy creates unpaid obligations that accumulate through the energy supply chain (this is exactly circular debt), while raising prices abruptly instead can hurt households and industry directly — genuinely good energy-policy design has to manage both of these pressures simultaneously, not treat them as separate problems.

Social-sector development covers health, education, social protection, and water and sanitation services — areas that build human capability directly. These are not merely welfare spending: better health and stronger learning outcomes raise labour productivity, labour-force participation, and long-run growth, which is why social-sector spending has a genuine economic, not only humanitarian, justification. The central issues are access, quality, equity, financing, the division of responsibilities between provincial and federal government, and implementation capacity. Example: building a new school physically increases access, but learning outcomes do not automatically improve unless teacher quality, student attendance, learning materials, and institutional accountability all function together — access alone is necessary but not sufficient.

Pakistan’s commonly cited major economic issues — the energy crisis, corruption, weak governance, external debt accumulation, unemployment, income inequality, inflation, fiscal and trade deficits, balance-of-payments pressure, and irrigation-water shortages — should be treated as one interconnected system, not as ten unrelated essay topics. Weak governance can reduce tax collection and the quality of public investment; fiscal deficits raise government borrowing needs; external imbalances increase financing pressure on the exchange rate; energy problems raise production costs across the whole economy; and low productivity together with weak human capital limits both export competitiveness and job creation. Example: a single energy-price shock can raise import costs, widen the trade deficit, increase inflation, raise pressure for fiscal subsidies, and weaken industrial competitiveness, all essentially at the same time — which is exactly why the issues above interact rather than sitting in separate boxes. Corruption itself is best analyzed through institutions, incentives, enforcement, and transparency, rather than treated as a moral slogan disconnected from its economic mechanisms. For any of these issues, a reliable answer structure is: current evidence, then root causes, then the economic transmission mechanism, then the groups or sectors affected, then possible reforms, then the practical constraints on implementing those reforms.

Paper II (Economics of Pakistan) key takeaways: always separate a long-run structural weakness from a temporary yearly shock before drawing a policy conclusion. Planning outcomes depend as much on institutional quality and implementation capacity as on the technical soundness of the plan itself. Agricultural and industrial policy both illustrate the same tension between short-run support (irrigation and credit access; import protection) and long-run competitiveness (water productivity and climate resilience; export orientation). Privatization only delivers its promised efficiency gains when it is paired with genuine post-sale competition and effective regulation. Pakistan’s major economic issues form one connected system, in which governance, fiscal, external, energy, and human-capital weaknesses continuously reinforce each other, so a credible reform proposal for any single issue has to acknowledge its links to the others.

items.text: Price elasticity of demand: percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in price (use the absolute value for classifying elastic versus inelastic demand)
National-income identity: Y = C + I + G + (X minus M)
Simple consumption function: C = a + bYd; simple saving: S = Yd minus C
Simple spending multiplier: k = 1/(1 minus MPC), under restrictive model assumptions
Present value: PV = FV/(1+r)^n; future value: FV = PV(1+r)^n
Quantity equation: MV = PY; Cambridge cash-balance form: M = kPY
